The Trust Project What is this? FARGO — A federal agency is not releasing witness interviews in the child sex abuse investigation into former North Dakota Sen. Ray Holmberg, including those involving the disgraced lawmaker's close friends. The U.S. Justice Department’s criminal division in a Thursday, Aug. 20, letter declined The Forum’s request for interview transcripts that federal agents conducted in the Holmberg case, nearly a year after the DOJ confirmed it received the Freedom of Information Act request Oct. 10, 2025. Citing federal law, the criminal division said the transcripts did not have an "overriding public interest” and that “disclosure of law enforcement records concerning an individual could reasonably be expected to constitute an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy.” ADVERTISEMENT “Because any nonpublic records responsive to your request would be categorically exempt from disclosure, this office is not required to conduct a search for the requested records,” the criminal division letter said. “Please be advised that we have considered the foreseeable harm standard.” The answer to The Forum’s request comes more than a year after Holmberg was sentenced to 10 years in federal prison for traveling to Prague multiple times between 2011 and 2016 with plans to sexually abuse children. The 82-year-old Republican pleaded guilty to the charge, and North Dakota U.S. Judge Daniel Hovland gave the former senator the maximum punishment on March 26, 2025. Acting U.S. Attorney Jennifer Puhl cross-examines a witness during the Wednesday, March 26, 2025, sentencing hearing for former North Dakota Sen. Ray Holmberg, center, at the Quentin N. Burdick U.S. Courthouse in Fargo. Trygve Olson / The Forum Holmberg is serving his sentence at the Federal Medical Center in Rochester, Minnesota. Federal records indicate he could be released Jan. 23, 2033. Holmberg, who lived in Grand Forks, served in the North Dakota Senate from 1977 to 2022. He resigned from office after The Forum reported he texted a jailed Nicholas Morgan-Derosier in April 2021. Morgan-Derosier was in the Grand Forks County Jail on child sex abuse materials, and Holmberg asked Morgan-Derosier to bring his 19- or 20-year-old boyfriend over for a massage, according to court transcripts. Morgan-Derosier is serving a 40-year sentence in federal prison for possessing, receiving and distributing child sex abuse material. Prosecutors claimed Morgan-Derosier sexually abused multiple children, though he was never charged in connection to those allegations. The letter from the DOJ doesn’t confirm whether the records The Forum requested exist. A North Dakota Bureau of Criminal Investigation report released a month after Holmberg's sentencing hearing said federal agents interviewed several of Holmberg’s close friends, including the late North Dakota Attorney General Wayne Stenehjem. Stenehjem died unexpectedly in late January 2022 from cardiac arrest, almost two months after federal agents interviewed the state’s top law enforcement agent Dec. 1, 2021. Stenehjem deleted three voicemails Holmberg left the late attorney general before and after the federal interview, current North Dakota Attorney General Drew Wrigley previously told The Forum. Stenehjem shared one of the messages with a Homeland Security agent, Wrigley said. ADVERTISEMENT “Wayne, this is my burner phone,” the message said. “I’m in big trouble. Don’t tell anyone." The BCI report also connected Holmberg to former University of North Dakota Center for Innovation CEO Bruce Gjovig. Holmberg sent Gjovig an email asking what he thought of the former senator’s “twink,” to which Gjovig said he was “too young.” “No one is ever to (sic) young… remembr (sic) Prague,” Holmberg replied back, according to the BCI documents. In a statement through his attorney, Gjovig said he never went to Prague and denied knowing about Holmberg’s criminal activity. Gjovig testified under oath in the Holmberg case as required by law, the statement said. Fargo businessman Jim Poolman also confirmed federal agents interviewed him in the case. The former UND Alumni Association and Foundation chairman and North Dakota insurance commissioner said he spoke with Homeland Security for about 30 minutes in September 2023 about the case, about a month before Holmberg was indicted. The two worked together for years, but Poolman said he knew nothing about Holmberg’s “heinous activities and (had) done nothing illegal.” READ MORE NORTH DAKOTA NEWS Employee dies after work-related medical incident at Casselton soybean plant 11h ago North Dakota officials push for tougher penalties for fleeing 1d ago Is the Fargo area getting another data center? 1d ago Comments Share Share this article News Reporting News Reporting Based on facts, either observed and verified firsthand by the reporter, or reported and verified from knowledgeable sources. Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Reuters UK security and counter-terrorism Analysis Far-right and Iran add to mix of terror threats UK faces – not to mention AI Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor Annual update from MI5 chief highlighted a complex cocktail that could have real-life consequences for Britain Tue 13 Oct 2026 13.58 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 14.31 EDT Share MI5’s annual threat update covers so much ground it is easy to feel anxious. The terror threat has become more diverse, with far-right anti-migrant threats on the rise; while Iran has now firmly emerged alongside Russia as a country seeking to undertake violent and deadly plots in the UK. “There is no law of physics dictating that rising state threats will be accompanied by diminishing terrorist threats,” MI5’s director general, Ken McCallum, said , although one of his core messages was that people and the country at large needed to focus on being more resilient. “In this new world, we should expect to be tested.” A key issue highlighted by McCallum was that years of anti-migrant, anti-Muslim hostility had now led to an increase in cases where people were “tipping into terrorist intent” – that is crossing the line from rhetoric to violence. It is a complex area, but one certainly fuelled by political hate narratives and online subcultures. It is also fuelled by toxic rhetoric from abroad. Authoritarian regimes, McCallum said, were investing heavily “in trying to distort and divide our society” – although he was too polite to mention that there is plenty of evidence that voices from the US led by X owner Elon Musk are keen to sow division in the UK too , as they post about flashpoint events such as the June rioting in Belfast and Southampton . View image in fullscreen Ken McCallum, MI5’s director general. Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA A second trend is that seemingly far-off conflicts, such as the wars the UK did not start in Ukraine or Iran , have a habit of rippling back home. It is less than eight months since the US and Israel attacked Iran, subsequently with a little help from Britain, but already Iran is trying to direct terror plots in the UK. Both MI5 and the counter-terror police may have to do a little better to explain precisely what five men from London were doing in a village next to RAF Fairford in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September, given that nothing of significance was found in the vans and nobody has been charged. But McCallum warned that Iran had “ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites” – a likely reference to Fairford. That came a day after the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was “almost certainly” behind the episode. It would be surprising if both were wrong. That is not the only possible example. At the beginning of October, two Iranians from Liverpool and Salford were charged , accused of trying to make a chlorine powder bomb to target Jewish sites in Manchester. Prosecutors alleged they were directed by a third party, believed to be in Iran. The two have not yet pleaded to the charges; a trial at the Old Bailey is scheduled. Rightwing extremists increasingly likely to consider terrorist attacks, MI5 chief says Read more Yet, if these fast-emerging threats were not enough, the normally sober McCallum decided to reference AI. He warned that AI could refine terror plots, supercharge hackers, produce individually targeted propaganda – and even help develop a novel bioweapon. This, he added, with emphasis, was a subject on which they were “particularly focused”, as if it was episode one of a TV thriller. While concerns were recently raised about scientists who have used AI to design viruses, as Anthropic warned of five examples of scientists who had used Claude for researching novel pathogens, both instances provoked a scientific debate as to what is actually possible. And what McCallum did not mention was that AI is also an extraordinary and potentially intrusive tool for MI5 to seek out threats. There is already enough for the intelligence agencies to think about, as the MI5 review makes clear: a country made more dangerous by blowback from strongmen starting what they think will be short wars; a rising tide of hatred that may start online but is morphing into violent intent in real life; a complex cocktail of external and internal threats that could have real-life consequences. As McCallum himself recognised: “The protection of democracy – its institutions, its representatives, its principles – has never felt more vital.” Explore more on these topics UK security and counter-terrorism MI5 Counter-terrorism policy Iran Russia The far right Europe analysis Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Russia did try to interfere in Brexit referendum, head of MI5 confirms MI5 warns UK universities over ‘theft of tech secrets by Chinese front company’ MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities MI6 is top European foreign intelligence service, peer review finds MI5 reprimanded for lying about ties with neo-Nazi informant who attacked girlfriend with machete MI5 apologises and pays compensation to woman allegedly abused by agent Britain caught in ‘space between peace and war’, says new head of MI6 Outgoing MI6 chief says Putin has ‘bitten off more than he can chew’ in Ukraine MI5 apologises after spy gave false evidence about neo-Nazi informant MI5 forced to ‘pare back’ counter-terrorism work due to rogue states, says chief Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A Lithuanian man is to stand trial next year for allegedly stabbing somebody in a south Essex neighbour dispute. Saulius Kursaitis, 48, of Grange Road in Bowers Gifford, pleaded not guilty on Tuesday (September 29) to inflicting grievous bodily harm (GBH) with intent. He is alleged to have wounded the man on August 28. He is also charged with assaulting a woman by beating her on the same date, to which he also pleaded not guilty through a Lithuanian interpreter. His trial was fixed for March 15. Until then, Judge Samantha Cohen told Basildon Crown Court, he will be remanded into custody. https://www.juneesoutherncross.com.au/st.text: Australian women's involvement at the China Open is down to just one singles player after Kimberly Birrell and Storm Hunter were both second-round casualties. World No.41 Birrell suffered a 6-4 6-4 loss to Czech Marie Bouzkova at the WTA 1000 event in Beijing on Saturday night. Birrell, 28, who won the Korea Open last Sunday with a win over compatriot Maya Joint in the final, raced out to a 3-1 first-set lead before dropping serve twice to lose it in 42 minutes. Down 3-0 in the second, Birrell lifted and won the next four games but was broken twice more to see her involvement in the Chinese capital come to a premature end. For Bouzkova, the 28-year-old 18th seed, a meeting with China's Zheng Qinwen awaits. The 2024 Olympic champion was leading Anna Kalinskaya 6-7 (4-7) 6-4 3-0 when the Russian retired. Earlier, Queensland veteran and former doubles world No.1 Storm Hunter was beaten 6-2 6-2 by Maria Sakkari in just 73 minutes. The 182nd-ranked Hunter failed to join 20-year-old fellow Aussie Taylah Preston in round three, losing serve six times in her latest hardcourt tournament clash in Asia. Next up for Sakkari, the Greek 25th seed and former world No.3, is Elina Svitolina. The sixth-seeded Ukrainian came from a set down to eliminate Czech Katerina Siniakova, 1-6 6-4 6-2. Shock of the day came with newly crowned world No.1 Elena Rybakina crashing out ‌3-6 6-4 6-3 to unseeded Alina Charaeva in the second round. It couldn't have been a worse start to her reign as the No.1 as Rybakina lost in her first match since defeating four-times major winner Aryna Sabalenka to capture the US Open title last month. Charaeva, a 24-year-old Russian-born Armenian ranked 118th ​in the world, etched her name into the record books by becoming the lowest-ranked competitor since the introduction of the WTA rankings in 1975 to rally from a set down to defeat a world No.1. Elsewhere, there were wins for third seed Coco Gauff, eighth seed Iga Swiatek, 21st seed Ann Li and 24th seed Jelena Ostapenko. Australian Associated Press
